1.pericope_label: Simon Peter, servant and apostle, to them that have obtained like precious faith with us

schools.summary: Report the ancient doubts about the authorship and their exact extent; argue from the Jewish and unusual form of the name both that the writer was a Jewish Christian and that, if not the apostle, he was no imitator; compare the reserve of the earlier letter’s opening with the personal designations here; weigh the divided manuscripts; and fix the sense of “like precious” as equal in honour and privilege rather than in value.

Reduce the question of authorship to a dilemma, the internal claims leaving only the apostle or a forgery; and read the readers’ faith as equal to that of eye-witnesses, obtained not by works but by free grace, through a righteousness both active and passive.
Explain the restoration of the circumcision name as tact toward Jewish believers zealous for the law, who might have taken its omission ill.

Distinguish the servant of Christ from the servant of sin; make the title of servant wider than that of apostle, covering every public minister, so that the apostleship is marked as a higher rank; and decline to explain why the name is given differently in the two epistles.

debates: Why the more Jewish form of the name stands here and not in the first epistle: as evidence bearing on authorship (Ellicott), as tact toward Jewish readers (Henry), or as something that simply does not appear (Calvin).
How far the ancient doubts about the letter reach — Barnes shows that the fathers who record them did not themselves reject it, while Clarke presses the alternatives to apostle or forgery.
Whether “like precious” means equal in value or equal in honour — Robertson distinguishes the two senses of the compound and chooses the second.
Whether the reserve of the first epistle’s opening and the fuller designations here need explaining at all, and what the difference shows (Ellicott alone draws an argument from it).
outliers: Ellicott alone makes one feature of the text tell in favour of authenticity and in favour of a non-apostolic author at the same time, and says so.
Clarke alone reduces the question to a bare dilemma admitting no third possibility.
Barnes alone insists on the difference between a book being disputed and a book being rejected.
Calvin alone treats the change of name as unexplained and leaves it so.

2.pericope_label: Grace and peace multiplied in the knowledge of God; his divine power; the exceeding great and precious promises

schools.summary: Render the preposition as marking a sphere and the noun as a fuller knowledge, set against heretical claims to a special one; refer the divine power to Christ and make the reference an argument for his deity; argue from epistolary convention that the third verse begins a new sentence; confine the life to the life of religion; and identify the promises as those of Christ’s return rather than of his coming.

Prefer “through” for the preposition; weigh Father and Son for the antecedent of the power and settle on the nearer; and locate the difficulty of the relative exactly, holding that it must be read of God’s own glory and power, with a lexical argument that the second word never means power.

Take the noun as acknowledgment rather than knowledge and draw a practical rule from it; include the present natural life in what is given; restrict the gifts to what the Spirit bestowed on the apostles; identify the promises with the whole inheritance of Israel transferred to Gentile readers; and read partaking of the divine nature as renewal in God’s image and mutual indwelling.
Read partaking of the divine nature sacramentally, the communicant being made of one body and blood with Christ and so bearing him in his members.

debates: What the preposition and noun of the second verse mean: sphere and fuller knowledge (Ellicott, Robertson), instrument (Calvin), or acknowledgment rather than knowledge at all (Clarke).

What the relative at the fourth verse refers to — the glory and virtue (Ellicott, Robertson, and Calvin, who says only that reading removes the ambiguity) or the things pertaining to life and godliness.
Which promises are meant: those of Christ’s return (Ellicott) or the promises made to Israel now extended to Gentiles (Clarke).
How men become partakers of the divine nature — by receiving the sacrament (Cyril) or by renewal in the image of God and mutual indwelling (Wesley).
Whether “life” includes the natural life (Wesley) or only the life of religion (Barnes), and whether “us” means Christians generally or the apostles (Clarke).
outliers: Robertson alone turns the reference of “his divine power” into an argument for the deity of Christ, and alone finds an anti-heretical motive in the word for knowledge.
Ellicott alone argues the punctuation from the practice of the canonical letters, and alone infers the writer’s temperament from his haste.
Calvin alone supports his construction with a lexical denial about the range of the word rendered virtue.
Cyril alone reads the promise of the divine nature as fulfilled in the eucharist.

5.pericope_label: Giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue, knowledge, temperance, patience, godliness, brotherly kindness, charity

schools.summary: Correct the opening phrase to “for this very reason” and blame the received English for hiding a parallel with the earlier epistle; describe the diligence as our contribution brought in alongside God’s gifts; correct the preposition so that the virtues are supplied in faith rather than added to it; and deny that the graces are to be acquired one after another in the order named.

Read the opening as a concession rather than a consequence, the diligence guarding against receiving grace in vain; hear a dance in the verb, the graces led up hand in hand in a beautiful order, each leading to the next and none lost as the next is gained; and take the first virtue as the courage needed to profess the faith under persecution.

Make the putting off of corruption an arduous labour leaving no room for sloth, the effort to be made evident to all; grant that supplying to faith is adding to faith while denying that any proper gradation is intended; and define temperance against a party that made salvation depend on knowledge whatever the life.

State the purpose of the letter, that a precious faith already obtained is a good beginning not to be rested in; and draw the rule that we must exhort those we pray for and press them to the means of what we ask God to give.

debates: Whether the opening phrase gives the reason for the diligence or concedes something in spite of which it is needed — Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley take it as a consequence of God’s gifts, Clarke as a caution against receiving them in vain.

Whether the graces form a graded chain: Wesley finds each leading to the next in order, Calvin denies any proper gradation, Barnes denies that they are acquired successively, and Ellicott removes the preposition that would make a chain, reading “in your faith supply virtue”.
What the first virtue is — goodness, or courage and fortitude for confessing the faith under persecution (Clarke, Wesley).
Whether the clause about temperance is aimed at a particular error — Gill alone names one.
outliers: Ellicott alone declares the received rendering of the opening indefensible and traces the faulty preposition to a single English version.
Calvin alone concedes the sense of the verb and then refuses the gradation everyone else builds on it.
Robertson alone reports the phrase from an ancient inscription.
Clarke and Wesley alone hear the figure of a dance in the word for adding.

8.pericope_label: If these things be in you and abound; make your calling and election sure; an entrance ministered abundantly

schools.summary: Correct the tautology of the received English; make election consequent on obedience to the heavenly calling and forfeitable if the graces are not added; promise that diligence secures against final falling; and report a variant reading of “consolation” for “calling”.

Prefer “idle” to “barren” and note the older English versions that had it; explain the rare word for short-sightedness; read the exhortation as concerning assurance under the uncertainty low attainment brings; define calling and election as two aspects of one fact, the invitation and the distinction it makes; and accept the sense of an inserted phrase while rejecting its authority.

Make the graces the test of a real knowledge of Christ, which is a living root that bears fruit; take the security of calling and election as evidence to ourselves rather than as anything added to the thing itself; observe that calling is named first though election is prior and weightier; and reject the inserted phrase as unauthorised and unnecessary.

debates: What it is to make one’s calling and election sure: proof to ourselves that the election was real (Calvin), assurance against the doubt low attainment creates (Barnes), a security that may be lost if the graces are not added (Clarke), or a firmness which if attained means one shall never finally fall (Wesley).
Whether election follows the calling or precedes it — Clarke makes it consequent on obedience to the call, Calvin makes it prior and the weightier of the two.
Whether the received “barren and unfruitful” is a tautology — Clarke, Ellicott, Barnes and Wesley all say it is.
How to treat the inserted words “by means of your works”: rejected as unauthorised and unnecessary (Calvin), rejected in authority but accepted in sense (Ellicott).
outliers: Clarke alone reports a manuscript reading “consolation” in place of “calling”.
Calvin alone explains why calling is named before election though election is the prior thing.
Wesley alone turns the test on the reader’s own history since pardon, and alone notices that the address “brethren” occurs at this point only in either epistle.
Barnes alone reads the eighth verse as encouragement rather than as a test.

12.pericope_label: I will not be negligent to put you in remembrance; shortly I must put off this tabernacle; that after my decease ye may remember

schools.summary: Correct the opening to a positive undertaking; deny that “the present truth” means the truth now under discussion, the literal rendering misrepresenting the sense; hold that the verse about the tabernacle concerns the swiftness of the death and not its nearness, or leave both senses open; deny that any revelation lies behind it; and list without deciding the conjectures about what the closing promise refers to.

Excuse the repetition on the ground that admonition in great matters is never superfluous; render the clause literally, short is the putting away of this tabernacle; and teach from it how far death differs from perdition, being a removal elsewhere and not a perishing.
Make the minister’s diligence the condition of the people’s, and take up the title of the Lord’s remembrancers in both directions, toward the people and toward God.

Give “the present truth” as the truth now being declared; think a fresh intimation of the approaching death likely while allowing that age and the old prediction would have sufficed; and find the promised provision fulfilled in the two epistles themselves.

debates: What “the present truth” means — Ellicott denies it is the truth now under discussion and calls the literal rendering misleading, which is exactly the sense Wesley gives it.

What the fourteenth verse asserts: that the writer’s death is near (Barnes, Clarke, Wesley) or that it will be swift when it comes, leaving no room for deathbed words (Ellicott), with Robertson allowing either.
Whether a fresh revelation of the approaching death is implied — Clarke and Wesley think it likely, Barnes denies it and infers from age alone.

What the promise of the fifteenth verse points to: this letter, copies of it, further letters, a Gospel written at his direction, or men commissioned to teach — Ellicott finds nothing to decide between them, while Barnes and Clarke take it of the writings.
outliers: Ellicott alone declares that only the earliest English version renders the fourteenth verse rightly, and alone refuses to choose among the explanations of the fifteenth.
Henry alone uses the title of remembrancer in both directions, of reminding God as well as the people.
Clarke alone sets a pagan philosopher’s answer about his burial beside the apostle’s language about his tabernacle.
Robertson alone notes that the word for decease is the word used on the mount of transfiguration, where the writer was present.

16.pericope_label: Not cunningly devised fables; eyewitnesses of his majesty; the voice from the excellent glory on the holy mount

schools.summary: Identify the fables with heathen tales of gods in human form and argue it from the technical term for those admitted to the mysteries; argue from motive that inventing such a story would have been not cunning but folly; and divide honour from glory, the first belonging to the voice and the second to the altered countenance.

Allow both Jewish and Gentile fables and connect the word with the metamorphoses of the gods, a transfiguration being about to be described; distinguish a declarative honour from the essential glory that admits no addition; and explain the visible display as making the voice more solemn, God having always added tokens of his presence to his words.

Refuse to specify which fables are meant, the negative being general; contrast proof by competent eyewitnesses with the reasoning by which Greek opinions were defended; refer both honour and glory to the voice and reject the division of them as forced; and note that the sentence is left without a finite verb.
Assert that the way of salvation is the counsel of God and no contrivance of men endeavouring by craft to deceive.
Draw from the Father’s declaration that a man who is not himself well pleased in the Son has not life, and that piety toward the Father requires the worship of the Son.

debates: Which fables are denied: heathen tales of gods in human form, argued from the word for those admitted to the mysteries (Clarke); Jewish and Gentile alike, with the metamorphoses chiefly in view (Gill); or none in particular, the denial being general (Ellicott).
Whether “honour and glory” both belong to the voice — Ellicott says they do and calls the alternative forced, while Clarke and Wesley take the second of the altered countenance.
What kind of honour the Son received — declarative rather than essential (Gill), against the plain reading of a bestowal.
How the denial of fable is to be made good: by the standing of the witnesses (Barnes) or by the absurdity of the supposed fraud (Wesley).
outliers: Clarke alone argues the sense of “fables” from the technical name given to initiates of the mysteries.
Wesley alone reasons from what the deceivers would have had to gain, and finds the supposed invention the greatest folly possible.
Ellicott alone declines to identify the fables and lists the proposals without choosing.
Robertson alone notes that the sentence is grammatically unfinished.

19.pericope_label: We have also a more sure word of prophecy, a lamp shining in a dark place, till the day dawn

schools.summary: Take the comparative at face value, so that prophecy is the stronger of the two proofs offered, and describe the Old Testament as a prophetic declaration of the Godhead, incarnation, power and coming of Christ.

Set out the competing constructions and find them all unsatisfactory, refusing to weigh the sacred writings against fables; deny the escape of taking the comparative for a positive; and read the “we” as covering teachers and disciples together, with Jewish readers chiefly in view.

Settle the sense from the meaning of the adjective, proved from five New Testament passages, so that the prophetic word is “more confirmed” by what happened on the mount; and draw out the figure of the lamp, the dark place being the whole ancient world outside one small spot, the daylight being the gospel and the morning star Christ risen in the heart.

Catalogue the proposed constructions, including one translator’s simple removal of the comparative; agree that the transfiguration confirmed the prophecies and mark the contrary view as less likely; note that the phrase occurs nowhere else and is used elsewhere of an uncanonical quotation; and confess that the sense of the sentence is not quite clear.

debates: What the prophetic word is called surer than: the fables (rejected by Gill), the apostolic eyewitness (Henry affirms it, Robertson calls it less likely, Gill says all reject it), or nothing at all, the comparative meaning “confirmed” by the transfiguration (Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott, Robertson).
Whether the comparative may be taken for a positive — proposed by some and reported by Barnes, denied by Calvin as inattentive to the context.
Whether the sense of the sentence can be settled at all — Ellicott, having chosen a rendering, admits it is not quite clear.
Who is included in “we” — the apostles only, or teachers and disciples together (Calvin), or all Christians (Wesley).
outliers: Clarke alone decides the question lexically, from the established sense of the adjective in five other passages.
Henry alone maintains that prophecy is a stronger proof than the vision on the mount.
Ellicott alone traces the phrase to an early writer’s citation of an uncanonical prophecy.
Wesley alone develops the lamp and the dark place into a comparison of the two Testaments.

20.pericope_label: No prophecy of Scripture is of private interpretation; holy men spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost

schools.summary: Concede that the disputed phrase has divided expositors as much as any in the New Testament and set out the constructions it will bear; decide it of the source rather than of the reader, against a confessional reading named and rejected; recover the antithesis between prophecy not being brought in by men and men being brought to speak by the Spirit; correct “in old time” to “at any time” and prefer a better-attested reading of the last clause; and note that the noun stands without the article.

Reach the same sense from the second meaning of the noun, as impulse, so that prophecy proceeds from no conjecture or private impulse of the prophet’s mind; and take the prophets to have been carried out of themselves and purely passive, receiving words above their own understanding whose intent they had to search out.

Report as almost universal the reading that forbids a reader to trust his own understanding, the Spirit being the only interpreter of himself, and call its doctrine true; but deny that the prophets were bereaved of mind as the heathen supposed of theirs, holding that they dared announce nothing of their own and followed the Spirit as their guide.

debates: Whether the disputed phrase concerns the reader’s exegesis or the prophet’s origination: Robertson and Clarke decide for the second, Calvin reports the first as the common view, Wesley makes God the interpreter, Ellicott lists three possibilities and Barnes declares the question unsettled.

How far the prophets were passive: carried out of themselves and ignorant of their own meaning (Clarke, Wesley) against Calvin’s express denial that they were bereaved of mind, being obedient rather than displaced.
Whether the clause means “not in old time” or “not at any time” — Ellicott corrects the received English and traces the error to one version.
Which reading closes the verse — Ellicott prefers a better-attested one that has men speaking from God.
outliers: Robertson alone names a confessional reading of the verse and rejects it by name.
Ellicott alone recovers the wordplay between the prophecy not being brought and the prophets being borne along.
Calvin alone contrasts the prophets with the ecstatic prophets of the heathen and refuses the comparison.
Clarke alone holds that the prophets did not know the intent of their own words.
